h1:
Sa Kaeo–Sa Khwan
The Ancient Ponds That Named the Town
intro: Plenty of people drive straight through Sa Kaeo town without realizing the province takes its name from two ponds that still sit right in the center of it. Sa Kaeo and Sa Khwan are ancient ponds said to have earned their names more than two hundred years ago, when a Thai army marched through on its way to campaign in Cambodia. Today they've become a public park where locals come to run, cycle, and sit by the water in the evening. We'll show you what's actually here, how to get to it, and why people in Sa Kaeo feel so attached to these two ponds.

blocks.html: Ask anyone in Sa Kaeo where the province name comes from and the answer is these two ponds — Sa Kaeo and Sa Khwan, ancient ponds that were here long before there was ever a province. They sit on the western side of town, inside Sa Kaeo–Sa Khwan Public Park, right next to the Sa Kaeo Municipal Office along Suwannason Road, around the kilometer 246–247 marker. Easy to find and right in town, so you don't have to drive far out the way you do for the province's other sights.

blocks.text: Where the name comes from — ponds an army once camped by

blocks.html: The story that's been handed down goes like this: around 1780, during the Thonburi period, Somdet Chao Phraya Maha Kasatsuek (later King Phra Phutthayotfa Chulalok, Rama I) was sent as commander to lead an army to campaign against Cambodia. On the way, the troops stopped to camp at these two ponds and drew water from them for the journey, so they named the pair Sa Kaeo and Sa Khwan. The names stuck and later became the name of the town, and then the province.

What makes these two ponds more than ordinary water is the belief that their water is pure and sacred. In the old days it was used in the royal Water Oath ceremony (the rite of drinking water to swear loyalty to the land), and in more recent times Sa Kaeo–Sa Khwan has been registered as one of the province's sacred water sources used in important royal ceremonies of the kingdom.

blocks.title: Why they're always named together
blocks.html: People always say Sa Kaeo and Sa Khwan as a pair because they're two ponds in the same place that got their names at the same time — not a single pond. When you actually visit, you'll see it as one wide stretch of water inside a single public park.

blocks.text: What the two ponds are today

blocks.html: Beyond their historical value, Sa Kaeo–Sa Khwan still does a real job in town life: it's a reservoir that supplies the tap water for the Sa Kaeo municipal area, and the land around it has been turned into a public park for people to relax in. In the morning and evening you'll see locals walking, running, cycling, and sitting by the water as a matter of routine. It's a green space in the middle of town that people genuinely use, not just a quick photo stop.

The park also doubles as the venue for the province's bigger events — traditional festivals, cultural fairs, and municipal activities on various occasions. Time your visit to land on an event and it gets especially lively; on a normal weekday it's quiet and calm, good for just sitting around.

items: Location — western side of Sa Kaeo town, along Suwannason Road (km 246–247), next to the Sa Kaeo Municipal Office
Vibe — a riverside public park with walking and cycling paths and places to sit; locals come to exercise morning and evening
Good for — a quick stop to take in the town's history, a leg stretch on the road, an evening stroll, or anyone who likes a quiet corner in town
Entry — it's a public park, free to enter, no admission fee

blocks.title: Best time to go
blocks.html: Come in the late afternoon around 4:30–6:30 pm, when the sun softens — you'll catch locals out exercising and lovely evening light on the water. The park does occasionally close part of the grounds for maintenance, so if you're set on walking the full loop around the ponds, it's worth checking the Sa Kaeo Municipality page first.

blocks.text: What to pair Sa Kaeo–Sa Khwan with

blocks.html: The nice thing about this spot is that it's right in town, so it works well as a starting point or a break before heading out to the sights farther afield. Twenty to forty minutes is enough to walk the ponds and read the history boards, then you can drive on to other places the same day.

items.name: Khao Chakan
items.blurb: A limestone mountain with caves, a troop of monkeys, and a cave temple. The highlight is the hundreds of thousands of bats streaming out of the cave around 6 pm. Not far from town, so it pairs well after the ponds.

items.name: Pang Sida National Park
items.blurb: Eastern forest close to town, with waterfalls you can reach on an easy walk and hundreds of butterfly species in June and July.

blocks.title: Getting there
blocks.html: Sa Kaeo–Sa Khwan is in the town center and easy to find, right next to the Sa Kaeo Municipal Office along Suwannason Road. If you drive yourself, parking is easy. The province's other sights, though, are spread across different districts and far apart, so the smoothest way to do it is with your own car or a rental for the day.

faq.q: Where does the name Sa Kaeo province come from?
faq.a: From two ancient ponds in the town center, Sa Kaeo and Sa Khwan. The story goes that around 1780, Somdet Chao Phraya Maha Kasatsuek (later King Rama I) led an army to campaign against Cambodia and stopped to camp at the two ponds, drawing water from them along the way. The troops named the ponds Sa Kaeo and Sa Khwan, and that became the name of the town and later the province.

faq.q: Where is Sa Kaeo–Sa Khwan and how do you get there?
faq.a: It's on the western side of Sa Kaeo town, inside Sa Kaeo–Sa Khwan Public Park, next to the Sa Kaeo Municipal Office along Suwannason Road around the kilometer 246–247 marker. It's right in town, so it's easy to find if you drive yourself, with easy parking.

faq.q: Why is the pond water considered sacred?
faq.a: Because it's been believed since ancient times that the water in Sa Kaeo–Sa Khwan is pure. It was used in the royal Water Oath ceremony, and in more recent times it has been registered as one of the province's sacred water sources used in important royal ceremonies of the kingdom.

faq.q: What can you do at Sa Kaeo–Sa Khwan now?
faq.a: It's a riverside public park in the middle of town. Locals come to walk, run, cycle, and sit by the water in the morning and evening. Entry is free, and it takes about 20–40 minutes to walk the ponds and read the history boards. It also serves as the municipality's tap-water reservoir and as a venue for the province's major events.

faq.q: When's the best time to visit?
faq.a: Late afternoon around 4:30–6:30 pm is a good time, when locals come out to exercise and the light on the water is lovely. Mornings are quiet and pleasant too. The park occasionally closes part of the grounds for maintenance, so if you're set on walking the full loop around the ponds, try checking the Sa Kaeo Municipality page first.
